newsitem.title: CUBA: Vatican foreign minister visits Cuba, bringing aid.
newsitem.headline: Vatican foreign minister visits Cuba, bringing aid.

text.p: Vatican Foreign Minister Jean Louis Tauran arrived in Cuba on Friday for a five-day visit that could lead to Pope John Paul's meeting President Fidel Castro and later coming himself to the communist-ruled island.
Tauran brought aid from the Pope for victims of Hurricane Lili and said he hoped his trip could help improve relations between the Roman Catholic Church and the Cuban state.

The first Vatican foreign minister to be invited to this Caribbean island by the government, Tauran was greeted at Havana airport by Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina and Cuban Cardinal Jaime Ortega after flying from Rome via Madrid.

He said he had met on Wednesday with the Pope, who was "very sad" about the effects of Hurricane Lili. The storm swept through central and western Cuba a week ago, destroying more than 5,000 homes and damaging crops and communications.

Tauran, speaking briefly at the airport, said the Pope had asked him to give the Cuban bishops financial aid for hurricane victims, calling this a sign of "the Pope's closeness and affection for all the Cuban people." He did not specify the size of the contribution.

He described the Cuban Catholic Church as "full of vitality, a courageous church that is not afraid to affirm its identity, and that as such is an even more important element in the public national dialogue in Cuba." The comment seemed to indicate that the Vatican would like to see the church able to play a more active role in Cuban society.

Tauran's visit could help prepare for a meeting between Castro and the Pope if the Cuban leader goes to Rome for a World Food Summit that the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation is holding there from Nov. 13 to 17.
Diplomatic sources in Rome have said that if Castro sees the Pope, he will probably invite him to Cuba, perhaps next year. The island is the only Latin American country the Pope has not visited.
Tauran did not mention the possibility of a Rome meeting in his airport statement. But he said he would like his visit to be a new milestone in Cuban-Vatican relations.
Earlier on Friday, Foreign Ministry spokesman Miguel Alfonso told a weekly news briefing that Tauran's trip should not be seen as "preparing for some other visit."

Cuban authorities have moved in recent years to improve relations with Christian churches, strained after Castro's 1959 revolution. But tension with the Catholic Church has persisted, particularly because of bishops' calls for political change.
Tauran is likely to meet Castro, although there has been no official confirmation that a meeting is planned. He is scheduled to see a series of senior government leaders.
